Madison, Wisconsin — full sun, average soil, 8 × 20 ft

WI — Wisconsin
Midwest & Great Lakes — EPA Level I: Eastern Temperate Forests / Great Plains
Tallgrass prairie, oak savanna and beech-maple forest. The richest palette in North America for sunny matrix planting: deep-rooted composites and warm-season bunchgrasses.
Likely USDA hardiness zone 4–5. Refined using the three-digit ZIP prefix. Confirm at planthardiness.ars.usda.gov.

12 combinations drawn from 163 species native to Midwest & Great Lakes that tolerate full sun and average soil in zone 4. Bed area 160 square feet. They are shown one at a time — use the buttons to page through them.

Downy Sunflower Seasonal 3–4 feet, yellow6. Golden Alexanders Seasonal 1.5–3 feet, yellow7. Narrowleaf Sundrops Seasonal 1–2 feet, yellow8. Little Bluestem Grass 2–4 feet, bronze9. Gray's Sedge Grass 2–2.5 feet, green10. Roundleaf Ragwort Groundcover 6–18 inches, yellow11. Woodland Strawberry Groundcover 4–8 inches, white12. Black-eyed Susan Filler 1.5–3 feet, yellow
Colours show what each plant is for, and match the Layer column in the table above. Plants doing the same job share a colour, so the numbers are what identify an individual species.
Every part of the bed is assigned to a species, so there is no bare ground to account for: the groundcover layer is drawn filling the gaps between the taller plants, which is exactly how it should be planted. Tallest species sit along the back edge and the shortest along the front. Numbers match the plant table, and each dot is one plant at its recommended spacing. Treat the shapes as drifts to copy freehand, not as a survey.

How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Plant one dominant grass as a continuous matrix 18 inches apart, then interrupt it with long tapering drifts of five to nine plants of each flowering species. Repeat two structural species at least three times each across the bed to create rhythm.

When to plant — zone 4, Midwest & Great Lakes
Best windowSpring, after the last hard frost — roughly mid May to mid June.
Second choiceLate summer, around mid August to mid September, also works, but it must be early enough that roots grow in before the ground freezes.
Why it mattersIn a zone this cold, spring is the safer choice. A plant put in late in autumn has not rooted enough to resist frost heave, and repeated freeze-and-thaw physically lifts the crown out of the soil over winter. If you do plant in autumn, mulch after the ground freezes, not before, to keep the soil temperature steady.
Your frost datesLast spring frost is typically mid May and first autumn frost late September in zone 4. These are regional averages — look up your own at frost dates by ZIP code, and treat your state Cooperative Extension planting calendar as the final word.
BuyingOrder plugs or quart pots in late winter for autumn delivery, since good native nurseries sell out of the better species months ahead. Small plants establish faster than large ones and cost a fraction as much — resist buying the biggest pot available.
Step by step
  1. Clear the ground and leave the soil alone. Kill or strip the existing turf and weeds completely — smother it under cardboard for a season, or lift the sod. Loosen only the top 2–3 inches so you can get a trowel in. Do not add fertiliser, and do not dig in compost deeper than a couple of inches. These are species adapted to ordinary unimproved soil; rich beds make them grow soft and flop. This bed is 20 feet by 8 feet, which is 160 square feet and takes 94 plants of 12 species, about one plant for every 1.7 square feet.
  2. Look each plant up before you buy it. Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 3 × Flat-topped Aster (Doellingeria umbellata, 3–6 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 2 × Rosinweed (Silphium integrifolium, 3–6 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 2 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  6. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 5 × Showy Goldenrod (Solidago speciosa, 2–4 feet) — 18 inches apart, as one drift of about 5 plants.
    • 3 × Smooth Blue Aster (Symphyotrichum laeve, 2–4 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Downy Sunflower (Helianthus mollis, 3–4 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 5 × Golden Alexanders (Zizia aurea, 1.5–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, as one drift of about 5 plants.
    • 7 × Narrowleaf Sundrops (Oenothera fruticosa, 1–2 feet) — 15 inches apart, as one drift of about 7 plants.
  7. Plant the matrix grass through and between everything you have already set out. This is the connective tissue of the planting: it should weave past the flowering drifts rather than sit in a separate block of its own.
    • 20 × Little Bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, 2–4 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 17 × Gray's Sedge (Carex grayi, 2–2.5 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  8. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 11 × Roundleaf Ragwort (Packera obovata, 6–18 inches) — 12 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 13 × Woodland Strawberry (Fragaria vesca, 4–8 inches) — 10 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Finally, scatter the self-sowing fillers into the gaps. Tuck them wherever there is still a hole. They are short-lived on purpose: they cover bare ground for the first two seasons while the permanent plants knit together, then fade out as the bed closes.
    • 5 × Black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta, 1.5–3 feet) — 15 inches apart, as one drift of about 5 plants.
  10. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  11. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

One cut a year, in early spring, after overwintering insects have emerged. No staking, no deadheading and no fertiliser: this planting is meant to hold itself up.

Your calendar — zone 4
  • Main cut-back window: mid to late April. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: mid May. Typical first autumn frost: late September.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 4. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Sedges — leave alone most years
Gray's Sedge

The sedge carpet is the part of this planting that replaces mulch, so disturb it as little as possible. Most years it needs nothing at all. If it accumulates brown thatch, shear it to 3 inches in mid to late April, or mow it on the highest mower setting, once every second or third year only.

Watering: Average. Sedges are shallow-rooted, so they show stress before anything else and make a useful indicator for the whole bed. If the carpet starts to look dull or straw-tipped, the bed wants water.

Warm-season grasses — one hard cut a year
Little Bluestem

These are the plants the phrase “cut the bed back” really applies to. Leave them standing all winter for structure and seed, then in mid to late April, before the new shoots are more than an inch or two high, cut the whole clump to 4–6 inches. Hedge shears or a string trimmer are fine. Cutting after growth starts leaves the clump with brown tips all season.

Watering: Low. Water weekly through the first summer only. After that these are among the most drought-proof plants in the bed, and watering them does more harm than good: it makes the clumps grow soft and flop open by late summer.

Evergreen perennials — tidy only, do not cut to the ground
Roundleaf Ragwort

These hold living leaves through winter and will be slow to recover if sheared hard. In mid to late April, pull or snip out only the dead and blackened leaves. Cut the spent flower stems off at the base. Every third year you can shear the top third to force fresh growth from the crown.

Watering: Average, but do not let them go bone dry in winter. Evergreen leaves keep losing water in cold weather, so in a long dry winter spell give them one soak while the ground is unfrozen.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
Flat-topped Aster, Rosinweed, Showy Goldenrod, Smooth Blue Aster, Downy Sunflower, Golden Alexanders, Narrowleaf Sundrops

Leave every stem standing all winter. In mid to late April, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Woodland Strawberry

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In mid to late April, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

Self-sowing fillers — decide where the seedlings go
Black-eyed Susan

These are short-lived by design and carry the bed while the slower plants fill in. Let the seedheads stand through winter for the birds. In mid to late April, shake the stems over any gap you want colonised, then cut them down. Through the season, pull seedlings out of the places you do not want them while they are still small.

Watering: Low. Water enough in the first few weeks to get them going, then leave them alone. Plants kept slightly lean set more seed, which for this layer is the whole point.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Spreads and will need editing: Downy Sunflower, Narrowleaf Sundrops, Roundleaf Ragwort, Woodland Strawberry. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 100 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 160 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for average soil
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: roughly that inch a week, counting rainfall, tapering off as autumn cools.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every two or three weeks during drought only. The bed should be largely self-sufficient by now.
  • Year 3 onward: water only in an exceptional drought, and even then only the ferns and the moisture-lovers. Everything else should be on its own.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
These will want water first and show it soonest: Flat-topped Aster, Golden Alexanders, Gray's Sedge. Use them as your indicator plants — when they wilt in the evening rather than perking back up, the bed needs a soak.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once or twice a week through the first growing season, then taper off. A long soak twice a week beats a daily sprinkle: it drives roots downward. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in mid to late April, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Warm-season bunchgrasses give skipper larvae host material, overwintering stems for cavity-nesting bees, and winter seed for sparrows.

Plant-by-plant notes
  • Doellingeria umbellata (Flat-topped Aster) — The larval host of Harris's checkerspot. Flat white plates for damp meadows. Looks like: 3–6 feet tall, upright stems with flat-topped flower heads, with white flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Silphium integrifolium (Rosinweed) — The shortest, tidiest Silphium for a sunny border. Long lived and deep rooted. Looks like: 3–6 feet tall, a big, coarse-textured plant with large leaves, with yellow flowers from July to September. Hardy in zones 4–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Solidago speciosa (Showy Goldenrod) — Clump forming, not running: the goldenrod for a designed bed. A keystone genus. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, an upright plant carrying flower spikes, with yellow flowers from August to October. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Symphyotrichum laeve (Smooth Blue Aster) — Smooth blue-green foliage resists mildew. Bluebird is a strong selection. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with light blue flowers from August to October. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Helianthus mollis (Downy Sunflower) — Velvety grey leaves. Rhizomatous: give it room or edge it with a mown strip. Looks like: 3–4 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with yellow flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 4–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Zizia aurea (Golden Alexanders) — The earliest yellow in a native border and a key nectar source for small spring bees. Looks like: 1.5–3 feet tall, upright stems topped with flat clusters of tiny flowers, with yellow flowers from April to June. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Apiaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Oenothera fruticosa (Narrowleaf Sundrops) — Bright yellow cups by day. Spreads by rosettes into a weed-proof mat. Looks like: 1–2 feet tall, a rounded, bushy mound, with yellow flowers from May to July. Hardy in zones 4–8; family Onagraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Schizachyrium scoparium (Little Bluestem) — Blue-green in summer, copper-orange in winter with silver seed. The best matrix grass. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, a stiff, erect clump, with bronze seedheads in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Poaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Carex grayi (Gray's Sedge) — Spiky mace-like seedheads used by flower arrangers. A strong clump for wet shade. Looks like: 2–2.5 feet tall, a small grassy tuft, with green seedheads from May to July. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Cyperaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Packera obovata (Roundleaf Ragwort) — Evergreen rosettes that knit into a weed-proof carpet in dry shade. Spreads by runners. Looks like: 6–18 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with yellow flowers from March to May. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Fragaria vesca (Woodland Strawberry) — Tiny sweet berries and a fast shade carpet. Spreads by runners. Looks like: 4–8 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with white flowers from April to July. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Rosaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Rudbeckia hirta (Black-eyed Susan) — Biennial or short-lived: treat it as a self-sowing filler that knits a young bed together. How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Sequence the seasonal layer so at least three species overlap in every month of the growing season. Group in odd-numbered drifts and let one colour repeat through the whole bed to hold it together.

When to plant — zone 4, Midwest & Great Lakes
Best windowSpring, after the last hard frost — roughly mid May to mid June.
Second choiceLate summer, around mid August to mid September, also works, but it must be early enough that roots grow in before the ground freezes.
Why it mattersIn a zone this cold, spring is the safer choice. A plant put in late in autumn has not rooted enough to resist frost heave, and repeated freeze-and-thaw physically lifts the crown out of the soil over winter. If you do plant in autumn, mulch after the ground freezes, not before, to keep the soil temperature steady.
Your frost datesLast spring frost is typically mid May and first autumn frost late September in zone 4. These are regional averages — look up your own at frost dates by ZIP code, and treat your state Cooperative Extension planting calendar as the final word.
BuyingOrder plugs or quart pots in late winter for autumn delivery, since good native nurseries sell out of the better species months ahead. Small plants establish faster than large ones and cost a fraction as much — resist buying the biggest pot available.
Step by step
  1. Clear the ground and leave the soil alone. Kill or strip the existing turf and weeds completely — smother it under cardboard for a season, or lift the sod. Loosen only the top 2–3 inches so you can get a trowel in. Do not add fertiliser, and do not dig in compost deeper than a couple of inches. These are species adapted to ordinary unimproved soil; rich beds make them grow soft and flop. This bed is 20 feet by 8 feet, which is 160 square feet and takes 117 plants of 12 species, about one plant for every 1.4 square feet.
  2. Look each plant up before you buy it. Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 5 × Flat-topped Aster (Doellingeria umbellata, 3–6 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as one drift of about 5 plants.
  6. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 2 × New England Aster (Symphyotrichum novae-angliae, 3–6 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 2 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Stiff Goldenrod (Solidago rigida, 3–5 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Swamp Milkweed (Asclepias incarnata, 3–5 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Downy Sunflower (Helianthus mollis, 3–4 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 5 × Pale Purple Coneflower (Echinacea pallida, 2–3.5 feet) — 18 inches apart, as one drift of about 5 plants.
    • 5 × Golden Alexanders (Zizia aurea, 1.5–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, as one drift of about 5 plants.
  7. Plant the matrix grass through and between everything you have already set out. This is the connective tissue of the planting: it should weave past the flowering drifts rather than sit in a separate block of its own.
    • 11 × Little Bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, 2–4 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 13 × Palm Sedge (Carex muskingumensis, 2–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  8. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 29 × Woodland Strawberry (Fragaria vesca, 4–8 inches) — 10 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 37 × Common Blue Violet (Viola sororia, 4–8 inches) — 8 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Finally, scatter the self-sowing fillers into the gaps. Tuck them wherever there is still a hole. They are short-lived on purpose: they cover bare ground for the first two seasons while the permanent plants knit together, then fade out as the bed closes.
    • 1 × Common Milkweed (Asclepias syriaca, 3–5 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as a single specimen.
  10. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  11. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

Leave all stems standing through winter. Cut back in spring in two passes a fortnight apart, so late-emerging insects are not destroyed all at once.

Your calendar — zone 4
  • Main cut-back window: mid to late April. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: mid May. Typical first autumn frost: late September.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 4. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Sedges — leave alone most years
Palm Sedge

The sedge carpet is the part of this planting that replaces mulch, so disturb it as little as possible. Most years it needs nothing at all. If it accumulates brown thatch, shear it to 3 inches in mid to late April, or mow it on the highest mower setting, once every second or third year only.

Watering: Average. Sedges are shallow-rooted, so they show stress before anything else and make a useful indicator for the whole bed. If the carpet starts to look dull or straw-tipped, the bed wants water.

Warm-season grasses — one hard cut a year
Little Bluestem

These are the plants the phrase “cut the bed back” really applies to. Leave them standing all winter for structure and seed, then in mid to late April, before the new shoots are more than an inch or two high, cut the whole clump to 4–6 inches. Hedge shears or a string trimmer are fine. Cutting after growth starts leaves the clump with brown tips all season.

Watering: Low. Water weekly through the first summer only. After that these are among the most drought-proof plants in the bed, and watering them does more harm than good: it makes the clumps grow soft and flop open by late summer.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
Flat-topped Aster, New England Aster, Stiff Goldenrod, Swamp Milkweed, Downy Sunflower, Pale Purple Coneflower, Golden Alexanders

Leave every stem standing all winter. In mid to late April, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Woodland Strawberry, Common Blue Violet

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In mid to late April, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

Self-sowing fillers — decide where the seedlings go
Common Milkweed

These are short-lived by design and carry the bed while the slower plants fill in. Let the seedheads stand through winter for the birds. In mid to late April, shake the stems over any gap you want colonised, then cut them down. Through the season, pull seedlings out of the places you do not want them while they are still small.

Watering: Low. Water enough in the first few weeks to get them going, then leave them alone. Plants kept slightly lean set more seed, which for this layer is the whole point.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Cut by half in early June: New England Aster. This is the one summer job that matters. Shortening these before they flower keeps them self-supporting, so you never need stakes.
  • Spreads and will need editing: Downy Sunflower, Palm Sedge, Woodland Strawberry, Common Blue Violet, Common Milkweed. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 100 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 160 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for average soil
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: roughly that inch a week, counting rainfall, tapering off as autumn cools.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every two or three weeks during drought only. The bed should be largely self-sufficient by now.
  • Year 3 onward: water only in an exceptional drought, and even then only the ferns and the moisture-lovers. Everything else should be on its own.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
These will want water first and show it soonest: Flat-topped Aster, New England Aster, Swamp Milkweed, Golden Alexanders, Palm Sedge. Use them as your indicator plants — when they wilt in the evening rather than perking back up, the bed needs a soak.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once or twice a week through the first growing season, then taper off. A long soak twice a week beats a daily sprinkle: it drives roots downward. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in mid to late April, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Prioritises plants documented as hosts for pollen-specialist native bees and as larval hosts for named butterflies and moths.

Plant-by-plant notes
  • Doellingeria umbellata (Flat-topped Aster) — The larval host of Harris's checkerspot. Flat white plates for damp meadows. Looks like: 3–6 feet tall, upright stems with flat-topped flower heads, with white flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Symphyotrichum novae-angliae (New England Aster) — Cut back by half in June for a self-supporting dome. A keystone genus. Looks like: 3–6 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with purple flowers from August to October. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Solidago rigida (Stiff Goldenrod) — Flat-topped heads and paddle leaves. Reliably upright, superb seed for juncos. Looks like: 3–5 feet tall, upright stems with flat-topped flower heads, with yellow flowers from August to October. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Asclepias incarnata (Swamp Milkweed) — Tolerates ordinary garden soil despite the name. Best milkweed for a tidy bed. Looks like: 3–5 feet tall, upright stems topped with flat clusters of tiny flowers, with pink flowers from June to August. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Apocynaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Helianthus mollis (Downy Sunflower) — Velvety grey leaves. Rhizomatous: give it room or edge it with a mown strip. Looks like: 3–4 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with yellow flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 4–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Echinacea pallida (Pale Purple Coneflower) — Drooping narrow rays, earlier than E. purpurea. Superb in lean soil. Looks like: 2–3.5 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with pale pink flowers from May to July. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Zizia aurea (Golden Alexanders) — The earliest yellow in a native border and a key nectar source for small spring bees. Looks like: 1.5–3 feet tall, upright stems topped with flat clusters of tiny flowers, with yellow flowers from April to June. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Apiaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Schizachyrium scoparium (Little Bluestem) — Blue-green in summer, copper-orange in winter with silver seed. The best matrix grass. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, a stiff, erect clump, with bronze seedheads in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Poaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Carex muskingumensis (Palm Sedge) — Whorled leaves like little palm trees. Spreads slowly to fill wet ground. Looks like: 2–3 feet tall, an arching, fountain-like clump, with tan seedheads in May and June. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Cyperaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Fragaria vesca (Woodland Strawberry) — Tiny sweet berries and a fast shade carpet. Spreads by runners. Looks like: 4–8 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with white flowers from April to July. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Rosaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Viola sororia (Common Blue Violet) — A keystone host genus for fritillary butterflies. It will colonise: use it as lawn and bed groundcover. Looks like: 4–8 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with violet flowers from March to May. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Violaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Asclepias syriaca (Common Milkweed) — Highly rhizomatous. Use only in large informal beds or a dedicated waystation. Looks like: 3–5 feet tall, a big, coarse-textured plant with large leaves, with pink flowers from June to August. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Apocynaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild

Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 2 × Flat-topped Aster (Doellingeria umbellata, 3–6 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 2 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Round-headed Bush Clover (Lespedeza capitata, 2–4 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  6. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 3 × Rough-stemmed Goldenrod (Solidago rugosa, 3–5 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Downy Sunflower (Helianthus mollis, 3–4 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 9 × Purple Milkweed (Asclepias purpurascens, 2–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, in 2 separate drifts of about 5 plants each.
    • 9 × Crooked-stem Aster (Symphyotrichum prenanthoides, 2–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, in 2 separate drifts of about 5 plants each.
    • 9 × Orange Coneflower (Rudbeckia fulgida var. sullivantii, 2–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, in 2 separate drifts of about 5 plants each.
  7. Plant the matrix grass through and between everything you have already set out. This is the connective tissue of the planting: it should weave past the flowering drifts rather than sit in a separate block of its own.
    • 16 × Little Bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, 2–4 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  8. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 15 × Wild Strawberry (Fragaria virginiana, 4–8 inches) — 12 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 43 × Western Dog Violet (Viola adunca, 2–6 inches) — 6 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Finally, scatter the self-sowing fillers into the gaps. Tuck them wherever there is still a hole. They are short-lived on purpose: they cover bare ground for the first two seasons while the permanent plants knit together, then fade out as the bed closes.
    • 7 × Whorled Milkweed (Asclepias verticillata, 1–2 feet) — 15 inches apart, as one drift of about 7 plants.
  10. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  11. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

Do not spray anything, ever, including organic Bt or spinosad. Leave milkweed stalks standing over winter.

Your calendar — zone 4
  • Main cut-back window: mid to late April. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: mid May. Typical first autumn frost: late September.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 4. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Warm-season grasses — one hard cut a year
Little Bluestem

These are the plants the phrase “cut the bed back” really applies to. Leave them standing all winter for structure and seed, then in mid to late April, before the new shoots are more than an inch or two high, cut the whole clump to 4–6 inches. Hedge shears or a string trimmer are fine. Cutting after growth starts leaves the clump with brown tips all season.

Watering: Low. Water weekly through the first summer only. After that these are among the most drought-proof plants in the bed, and watering them does more harm than good: it makes the clumps grow soft and flop open by late summer.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
Flat-topped Aster, Round-headed Bush Clover, Rough-stemmed Goldenrod, Downy Sunflower, Purple Milkweed, Crooked-stem Aster, Orange Coneflower

Leave every stem standing all winter. In mid to late April, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Wild Strawberry, Western Dog Violet

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In mid to late April, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

Self-sowing fillers — decide where the seedlings go
Whorled Milkweed

These are short-lived by design and carry the bed while the slower plants fill in. Let the seedheads stand through winter for the birds. In mid to late April, shake the stems over any gap you want colonised, then cut them down. Through the season, pull seedlings out of the places you do not want them while they are still small.

Watering: Low. Water enough in the first few weeks to get them going, then leave them alone. Plants kept slightly lean set more seed, which for this layer is the whole point.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Spreads and will need editing: Downy Sunflower, Crooked-stem Aster, Whorled Milkweed. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 100 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 160 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for average soil
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: roughly that inch a week, counting rainfall, tapering off as autumn cools.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every two or three weeks during drought only. The bed should be largely self-sufficient by now.
  • Year 3 onward: water only in an exceptional drought, and even then only the ferns and the moisture-lovers. Everything else should be on its own.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
These will want water first and show it soonest: Flat-topped Aster, Rough-stemmed Goldenrod, Orange Coneflower. Use them as your indicator plants — when they wilt in the evening rather than perking back up, the bed needs a soak.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once or twice a week through the first growing season, then taper off. A long soak twice a week beats a daily sprinkle: it drives roots downward. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in mid to late April, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Monarch Watch certifies waystations of 100 sq ft or larger carrying at least ten milkweed plants of two or more species plus continuous nectar.

Plant-by-plant notes
  • Doellingeria umbellata (Flat-topped Aster) — The larval host of Harris's checkerspot. Flat white plates for damp meadows. Looks like: 3–6 feet tall, upright stems with flat-topped flower heads, with white flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Lespedeza capitata (Round-headed Bush Clover) — Silvery buttons turn rich brown and hold all winter. Quail and sparrow seed. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, an upright plant carrying flower spikes, with cream flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Fabaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Solidago rugosa (Rough-stemmed Goldenrod) — The cultivar Fireworks sprays horizontally. A keystone genus for Lepidoptera. Looks like: 3–5 feet tall, an arching, fountain-like clump, with yellow flowers from August to October. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Helianthus mollis (Downy Sunflower) — Velvety grey leaves. Rhizomatous: give it room or edge it with a mown strip. Looks like: 3–4 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with yellow flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 4–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Asclepias purpurascens (Purple Milkweed) — The richest-coloured eastern milkweed. Slow to establish, then long lived at a woodland edge. Looks like: 2–3 feet tall, upright stems topped with flat clusters of tiny flowers, with magenta flowers from May to July. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Apocynaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Symphyotrichum prenanthoides (Crooked-stem Aster) — Zigzag stems and pale flowers for moist part shade. Spreads modestly. Looks like: 2–3 feet tall, an airy, see-through plant on fine stems, with pale lavender flowers from August to October. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Rudbeckia fulgida var. sullivantii (Orange Coneflower) — Long bloom and a clean basal rosette. The cultivar Goldsturm is this species. Looks like: 2–3 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with yellow flowers from July to October. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Schizachyrium scoparium (Little Bluestem) — Blue-green in summer, copper-orange in winter with silver seed. The best matrix grass. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, a stiff, erect clump, with bronze seedheads in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Poaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Fragaria virginiana (Wild Strawberry) — A fast-running edible groundcover and high-value host genus. Excellent green mulch in sun. Looks like: 4–8 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with white flowers from April to June. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Rosaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Viola adunca (Western Dog Violet) — The host of the threatened Oregon silverspot and several western fritillaries. Looks like: 2–6 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with violet flowers from April to June. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Violaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Asclepias verticillata (Whorled Milkweed) — Fine needle foliage, spreads by rhizome: a useful late-season monarch host. Looks like: 1–2 feet tall, a finely textured, almost ferny plant, with white flowers from July to September. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Apocynaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild

How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Choose one sedge as a unifying carpet and plant it 10 inches apart across the whole bed, then set ferns in loose groups of three to seven and drop clumps of shade perennials into the gaps. Texture does the work that flower colour does in sun.

When to plant — zone 7, Southeast (Piedmont, Coastal Plain, Gulf)
Best windowAutumn, roughly September to late October — about six weeks before your first hard frost, which here is typically late October.
Second choiceSpring, around early April to mid May, is the good second choice and is when nurseries have the widest selection.
Why it mattersAutumn planting is better because the soil is still warm while the air is cooling, so roots keep growing after the top has stopped, and the plant faces its first summer already anchored. Avoid planting in midsummer heat unless you can commit to watering every few days.
Your frost datesLast spring frost is typically mid April and first autumn frost late October in zone 7. These are regional averages — look up your own at frost dates by ZIP code, and treat your state Cooperative Extension planting calendar as the final word.
BuyingOrder plugs or quart pots in late winter for autumn delivery, since good native nurseries sell out of the better species months ahead. Small plants establish faster than large ones and cost a fraction as much — resist buying the biggest pot available.
Step by step
  1. Clear the ground and leave the soil alone. Kill or strip the existing turf and weeds completely — smother it under cardboard for a season, or lift the sod. Loosen only the top 2–3 inches so you can get a trowel in. Do not add fertiliser, and do not dig in compost deeper than a couple of inches. These are species adapted to ordinary unimproved soil; rich beds make them grow soft and flop. This bed is 14 feet by 6 feet, which is 84 square feet and takes 100 plants of 6 species, about 1.2 plants per square foot.
  2. Look each plant up before you buy it. Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 3 × False Solomon's Seal (Maianthemum racemosum, 2–3 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  6. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 3 × Poke Milkweed (Asclepias exaltata, 3–5 feet) — 18 inches apart, as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Elm-leaved Goldenrod (Solidago ulmifolia, 2–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  7. Place the ferns in loose groups of three to seven. Tuck them where they will be shaded in the afternoon, and against the base of taller plants rather than out in the open.
    • 29 × Broad Beech Fern (Phegopteris hexagonoptera, 1–2 feet) — 12 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  8. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 13 × White Wood Aster (Eurybia divaricata, 1–2 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 49 × Common Blue Violet (Viola sororia, 4–8 inches) — 8 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  10. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

No mulch and no leaf removal. Cut deciduous ferns down in late winter; shear evergreen sedges to 3 inches in early spring every second or third year.

What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Deciduous ferns — remove old fronds before the new ones uncurl
Broad Beech Fern

The fronds collapse over winter and protect the crown, so leave them. Cut them off at the base in mid to late March, before the new fiddleheads unroll. Once the fiddleheads are up, cutting anywhere near them damages the whole season's growth.

Watering: The highest need in the bed. Ferns have little ability to hold water and crisp irreversibly once they dry out. Keep the soil evenly damp but never waterlogged, and water in any dry spell longer than about ten days, even years later.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
False Solomon's Seal, Poke Milkweed, Elm-leaved Goldenrod, White Wood Aster

Leave every stem standing all winter. In mid to late March, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Common Blue Violet

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In mid to late March, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: roughly that inch a week, counting rainfall, tapering off as autumn cools.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every two or three weeks during drought only. The bed should be largely self-sufficient by now.
  • Year 3 onward: water only in an exceptional drought, and even then only the ferns and the moisture-lovers. Everything else should be on its own.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once or twice a week through the first growing season, then taper off. A long soak twice a week beats a daily sprinkle: it drives roots downward. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in mid to late March, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Carex is among the most important larval host genera for skippers and satyrs, and a dense sedge carpet outcompetes garlic mustard and stiltgrass.

Plant-by-plant notes
  • Maianthemum racemosum (False Solomon's Seal) — Plumes of white become ruby berries. A strong arching form for the shade middle ground. Looks like: 2–3 feet tall, an arching, fountain-like clump, with white flowers in May and June. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asparagaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Asclepias exaltata (Poke Milkweed) — The only milkweed for part shade. Drooping starry umbels under open trees. Looks like: 3–5 feet tall, upright stems topped with flat clusters of tiny flowers, with white and pale pink flowers in June and July. Hardy in zones 3–7; family Apocynaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Solidago ulmifolia (Elm-leaved Goldenrod) — A shade goldenrod with sprays of yellow at a woodland edge. Clump-forming. Looks like: 2–3 feet tall, an arching, fountain-like clump, with yellow flowers from August to October. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Phegopteris hexagonoptera (Broad Beech Fern) — Triangular fronds held horizontally. Spreads slowly to make a soft shade carpet. Looks like: 1–2 feet tall, a low, wide-spreading plant, grown for its foliage. Hardy in zones 4–8; family Thelypteridaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
