How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Build the composition from leaf shape, not flower colour: set one bold, broad-leaved or arching species against a fine-textured fern and a strappy sedge, then repeat that trio three or four times down the bed. Keep flowers pale so they read in low light.

When to plant — zone 7, Southeast (Piedmont, Coastal Plain, Gulf)
Best windowAutumn, roughly September to late October — about six weeks before your first hard frost, which here is typically late October.
Second choiceSpring, around early April to mid May, is the good second choice and is when nurseries have the widest selection.
Why it mattersAutumn planting is better because the soil is still warm while the air is cooling, so roots keep growing after the top has stopped, and the plant faces its first summer already anchored. Avoid planting in midsummer heat unless you can commit to watering every few days.
Your frost datesLast spring frost is typically mid April and first autumn frost late October in zone 7. These are regional averages — look up your own at frost dates by ZIP code, and treat your state Cooperative Extension planting calendar as the final word.
BuyingOrder plugs or quart pots in late winter for autumn delivery, since good native nurseries sell out of the better species months ahead. Small plants establish faster than large ones and cost a fraction as much — resist buying the biggest pot available.
Step by step
  1. Clear the ground and leave the soil alone. Kill or strip the existing turf and weeds completely — smother it under cardboard for a season, or lift the sod. Loosen only the top 2–3 inches so you can get a trowel in. Do not add fertiliser, and do not dig in compost deeper than a couple of inches. These are species adapted to ordinary unimproved soil; rich beds make them grow soft and flop. This bed is 14 feet by 6 feet, which is 84 square feet and takes 32 plants of 6 species, about one plant for every 2.6 square feet.
  2. Look each plant up before you buy it. Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 5 × Solomon's Seal (Polygonatum biflorum, 1.5–4 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as one drift of about 5 plants.
  6. Set out the shrub backbone first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 1 × Mapleleaf Viburnum (Viburnum acerifolium, 3–6 feet) — 42 inches apart (about 3.5 feet), as a single specimen.
  7. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 3 × Poke Milkweed (Asclepias exaltata, 3–5 feet) — 18 inches apart, as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Blue-stemmed Goldenrod (Solidago caesia, 1.5–3 feet) — 18 inches apart, as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  8. Place the ferns in loose groups of three to seven. Tuck them where they will be shaded in the afternoon, and against the base of taller plants rather than out in the open.
    • 3 × Goldie's Wood Fern (Dryopteris goldiana, 3–4 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 17 × White Wood Aster (Eurybia divaricata, 1–2 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  10. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  11. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

No mulch once the groundcover knits. Cut deciduous material down in late winter and top-dress with leaf mould, never bark.

Your calendar — zone 7
  • Main cut-back window: mid to late March. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: mid April. Typical first autumn frost: late October.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 7. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Spring-flowering shrubs — prune right after they bloom, or not at all
Mapleleaf Viburnum

Never cut these back with the perennials: the flower buds for next spring form on this year's wood over summer, so a late-winter cut removes the entire display. Most need no pruning at all. When one outgrows its space, prune within a few weeks of the flowers fading: remove whole stems at the base rather than shearing the outline.

Watering: Deep and infrequent, for two full years. Give each shrub a long slow soak at the root ball once a week through its first two summers rather than a light sprinkle, so the water reaches the bottom of the roots. After that, only in real drought.

Deciduous ferns — remove old fronds before the new ones uncurl
Goldie's Wood Fern

The fronds collapse over winter and protect the crown, so leave them. Cut them off at the base in mid to late March, before the new fiddleheads unroll. Once the fiddleheads are up, cutting anywhere near them damages the whole season's growth.

Watering: The highest need in the bed. Ferns have little ability to hold water and crisp irreversibly once they dry out. Keep the soil evenly damp but never waterlogged, and water in any dry spell longer than about ten days, even years later.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
Solomon's Seal, Poke Milkweed, Blue-stemmed Goldenrod, White Wood Aster

Leave every stem standing all winter. In mid to late March, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Spreads and will need editing: White Wood Aster. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 52 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 84 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for average soil
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: roughly that inch a week, counting rainfall, tapering off as autumn cools.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every two or three weeks during drought only. The bed should be largely self-sufficient by now.
  • Year 3 onward: water only in an exceptional drought, and even then only the ferns and the moisture-lovers. Everything else should be on its own.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
These will want water first and show it soonest: Goldie's Wood Fern. Use them as your indicator plants — when they wilt in the evening rather than perking back up, the bed needs a soak.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once or twice a week through the first growing season, then taper off. A long soak twice a week beats a daily sprinkle: it drives roots downward. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in mid to late March, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Deep shade beds are where most caterpillars pupate. A closed herbaceous layer plus retained leaf litter completes a life cycle that a bare mulched bed interrupts.

How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Excavate 4 inches and backfill with clean 3/8-inch crushed gravel, planting into the gravel with roots in the soil beneath. Keep everything low and let two or three spiky or rosette forms stand as punctuation.

When to plant — zone 8, Southwest Deserts
Best windowAutumn, about October to late November, once the worst heat has broken.
Second choiceThe summer monsoon, if your area gets one, is the other good window: plant into moist ground in July or August and the rains establish it for you.
Why it mattersAutumn planting gives roots the whole cool season to grow before the first brutal summer. Avoid planting from April to June, when a new plant cannot take up water fast enough to replace what the heat pulls out of it.
Your frost datesLast spring frost is typically late March and first autumn frost mid November in zone 8. These are regional averages — look up your own at frost dates by ZIP code, and treat your state Cooperative Extension planting calendar as the final word.
BuyingOrder plugs or quart pots in late winter for autumn delivery, since good native nurseries sell out of the better species months ahead. Small plants establish faster than large ones and cost a fraction as much — resist buying the biggest pot available.
Step by step
  1. Clear the ground and leave the soil alone. Kill or strip the existing turf and weeds completely — smother it under cardboard for a season, or lift the sod. Loosen only the top 2–3 inches so you can get a trowel in. Do not add compost, topsoil or fertiliser. Every plant in this design needs lean, sharp-draining ground, and enriching the soil is what kills them. This bed is 25 feet by 10 feet, which is 250 square feet and takes 146 plants of 13 species, about one plant for every 1.7 square feet.
  2. Look each plant up before you buy it. Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 3 × Soapweed Yucca (Yucca glauca, 1.5–3 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 3 × Parry's Agave (Agave parryi, 1.5–2.5 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  6. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 3 × Desert Globemallow (Sphaeralcea ambigua, 2–3.5 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
    • 9 × Silvery Lupine (Lupinus argenteus, 1–2.5 feet) — 18 inches apart, in 2 separate drifts of about 5 plants each.
    • 5 × Gregg's Mistflower (Conoclinium greggii, 1–2 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as one drift of about 5 plants.
    • 20 × Zizotes Milkweed (Asclepias oenotheroides, 6–18 inches) — 12 inches apart, in 3 separate drifts of about 7 plants each.
  7. Plant the matrix grass through and between everything you have already set out. This is the connective tissue of the planting: it should weave past the flowering drifts rather than sit in a separate block of its own.
    • 5 × Bull Grass (Muhlenbergia emersleyi, 2–3.5 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 25 × Sideoats Grama (Bouteloua curtipendula, 1.5–2.5 feet) — 15 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  8. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 25 × Sulphur Buckwheat (Eriogonum umbellatum, 6–18 inches) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 11 × Fringed Sage (Artemisia frigida, 6–18 inches) — 15 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 15 × Desert Zinnia (Zinnia acerosa, 4–8 inches) — 12 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
    • 15 × Frogfruit (Phyla nodiflora, 2–4 inches) — 12 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Finally, scatter the self-sowing fillers into the gaps. Tuck them wherever there is still a hole. They are short-lived on purpose: they cover bare ground for the first two seasons while the permanent plants knit together, then fade out as the bed closes.
    • 7 × Arroyo Lupine (Lupinus succulentus, 1–3 feet) — 12 inches apart, as one drift of about 7 plants.
  10. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  11. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Top the whole bed with 2–3 inches of clean gravel or coarse grit, keeping it clear of the plant crowns. Never use bark or compost on this design. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

Water only to establish, then stop entirely. Never mulch with compost or bark, which destroys the effect and rots the crowns.

Your calendar — zone 8
  • Main cut-back window: early to mid March. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: late March. Typical first autumn frost: mid November.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 8. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Agaves, yuccas and other rosettes — never cut back
Soapweed Yucca, Parry's Agave

There is no cutting back, ever. Cutting the leaves destroys the shape permanently, because each rosette grows from a single central point. Pull off only the dry, papery lower leaves, and saw the spent flower stalk off near the base once it has dried. Keep mulch and groundcover pulled back from the crown so water drains away from it.

Watering: Almost none, and overwatering is the real danger. Water once a month in the first summer only, then leave them to the rain. Never let water stand in the centre of a rosette, and never run an irrigation line to one.

Woody-based subshrubs — trim, never cut into the old wood
Sulphur Buckwheat, Fringed Sage, Desert Zinnia

These look like perennials but are built like tiny shrubs, and they regrow from their woody stems rather than from the crown. Cutting them to the ground usually kills them. In early to mid March, shorten the previous year's growth by about a third, always leaving green growth or live buds below your cut. Replace them every five to eight years as they go woody and open at the base.

Watering: Low, and sharp drainage matters more than water ever does. Soak once a week through the first summer, then stop almost completely. These rot at the crown in soil that stays damp, which is the usual way they are killed.

Warm-season grasses — one hard cut a year
Bull Grass, Sideoats Grama

These are the plants the phrase “cut the bed back” really applies to. Leave them standing all winter for structure and seed, then in early to mid March, before the new shoots are more than an inch or two high, cut the whole clump to 4–6 inches. Hedge shears or a string trimmer are fine. Cutting after growth starts leaves the clump with brown tips all season.

Watering: Low. Water weekly through the first summer only. After that these are among the most drought-proof plants in the bed, and watering them does more harm than good: it makes the clumps grow soft and flop open by late summer.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
Desert Globemallow, Silvery Lupine, Gregg's Mistflower

Leave every stem standing all winter. In early to mid March, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Zizotes Milkweed, Frogfruit

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In early to mid March, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

Self-sowing fillers — decide where the seedlings go
Arroyo Lupine

These are short-lived by design and carry the bed while the slower plants fill in. Let the seedheads stand through winter for the birds. In early to mid March, shake the stems over any gap you want colonised, then cut them down. Through the season, pull seedlings out of the places you do not want them while they are still small.

Watering: Low. Water enough in the first few weeks to get them going, then leave them alone. Plants kept slightly lean set more seed, which for this layer is the whole point.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Plant once and never move: Silvery Lupine, Zizotes Milkweed. These make a deep taproot and rarely survive being dug up and relocated. Buy them small.
  • Spreads and will need editing: Gregg's Mistflower, Frogfruit. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 156 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 250 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for a dry bed
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: one deep soak a week in hot weather, and skip it whenever the soil is damp two inches down. Err on the dry side from the start.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every three or four weeks during a heat wave, and otherwise nothing.
  • Year 3 onward: stop watering entirely. Continued summer irrigation is the main way established dry-soil plantings are lost.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once a week for the first summer only, then stop. These species fail from too much water far more often than too little. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in early to mid March, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Bare mineral ground between plants is prime nesting habitat for the roughly 70 percent of native bee species that nest in the soil.

Plant-by-plant notes
  • Yucca glauca (Soapweed Yucca) — The cold-hardiest yucca, from the shortgrass prairie. Looks like: 1.5–3 feet tall, a stiff, spiky architectural rosette, with cream flowers from May to July. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asparagaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Agave parryi (Parry's Agave) — A perfect blue-grey artichoke rosette: the strongest single focal form in a desert bed. Looks like: 1.5–2.5 feet tall, a symmetrical rosette, grown for its evergreen foliage. Hardy in zones 5–10; family Asparagaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Sphaeralcea ambigua (Desert Globemallow) — Silver-grey felted leaves and apricot cups nearly year-round with occasional water. Looks like: 2–3.5 feet tall, an upright plant carrying flower spikes, with apricot flowers from March to October. Hardy in zones 5–10; family Malvaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Lupinus argenteus (Silvery Lupine) — Silver-haired leaves and blue spikes on dry slopes. Taproot: plant small and never move it. Looks like: 1–2.5 feet tall, an upright plant carrying flower spikes, with blue flowers in June and July. Hardy in zones 3–7; family Fabaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild Zone 8 is one step above its published limit of 7: workable in most cases, but site it in the coolest part of the bed.
  • Conoclinium greggii (Gregg's Mistflower) — The famous Queen butterfly magnet, with lacy leaves and fuzzy lavender heads. Spreads by rhizome. Looks like: 1–2 feet tall, a rounded, bushy mound, with lavender flowers from April to November. Hardy in zones 7–10; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Asclepias oenotheroides (Zizotes Milkweed) — A low, sprawling Texas milkweed that flushes after rain. Taproot. Looks like: 6–18 inches tall, upright stems topped with flat clusters of tiny flowers, with greenish flowers from April to October. Hardy in zones 7–10; family Apocynaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Muhlenbergia emersleyi (Bull Grass) — A big glossy fountain with rose-purple plumes: rare among grasses for desert part shade. Looks like: 2–3.5 feet tall, a fountain of fine foliage, with purple and pink seedheads from August to October. Hardy in zones 6–10; family Poaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Bouteloua curtipendula (Sideoats Grama) — Oat-like seeds hang along one side of the stem. Fast, tough and fine textured. Looks like: 1.5–2.5 feet tall, a stiff, erect clump, with purple and tan seedheads from June to August. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Poaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Eriogonum umbellatum (Sulphur Buckwheat) — Buckwheats host an enormous range of butterflies. Flowers age from sulphur to rust. Looks like: 6–18 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with yellow and rust flowers from June to August. Hardy in zones 4–8; family Polygonaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Artemisia frigida (Fringed Sage) — A silky silver mat for gravel gardens. Do not cut into the old woody base. Looks like: 6–18 inches tall, a rounded, bushy mound, with silver flowers in August and September. Hardy in zones 2–8; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Zinnia acerosa (Desert Zinnia) — A tiny white-flowered subshrub for the hottest gravel gardens. Looks like: 4–8 inches tall, a rounded, bushy mound, with white flowers from May to October. Hardy in zones 7–10; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Phyla nodiflora (Frogfruit) — A creeping, flowering groundcover that takes traffic and flooding. Spreads by runners. Looks like: 2–4 inches tall, a flat, ground-hugging mat, with white and pink flowers from March to November. Hardy in zones 7–11; family Verbenaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Lupinus succulentus (Arroyo Lupine) — A fast annual lupine with blue spikes. Sow in autumn and let it reseed. Looks like: 1–3 feet tall, an upright plant carrying flower spikes, with blue flowers from February to May. Hardy in zones 7–10; family Fabaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild

Planting plan — 25 feet × 10 feet (250 square feet)

1. Havard's Penstemon Structural 3–6 feet, red2. Red Yucca Structural 2–4 feet, coral3. California Goldenrod Seasonal 2–4 feet, yellow4. Parry's Penstemon Seasonal 2–4 feet, pink5. Pineneedle Milkweed Seasonal 1–3 feet, white6. Engelmann Daisy Seasonal 1.5–3 feet, yellow7. Gregg's Mistflower Seasonal 1–2 feet, lavender8. Golden Prairie Clover Seasonal 1–2 feet, yellow9. Little Bluestem Grass 2–4 feet, bronze10. Scarlet Globemallow Groundcover 6–12 inches, orange11. Deerweed Filler 2–4 feet, yellow
Colours show what each plant is for, and match the Layer column in the table above. Plants doing the same job share a colour, so the numbers are what identify an individual species.
Every part of the bed is assigned to a species, so there is no bare ground to account for: the groundcover layer is drawn filling the gaps between the taller plants, which is exactly how it should be planted. Tallest species sit along the back edge and the shortest along the front. Numbers match the plant table, and each dot is one plant at its recommended spacing. Treat the shapes as drifts to copy freehand, not as a survey.

How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Include at least two milkweed species so host plants are available over a longer window, plus heavy late-season nectar. Site it in full sun out of the wind, with a shallow damp patch of bare mineral soil for puddling.

When to plant — zone 8, Southwest Deserts

    • 7 × Gregg's Mistflower (Conoclinium greggii, 1–2 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as one drift of about 7 plants.
    • 24 × Golden Prairie Clover (Dalea aurea, 1–2 feet) — 12 inches apart, in 4 separate drifts of about 6 plants each.
  7. Plant the matrix grass through and between everything you have already set out. This is the connective tissue of the planting: it should weave past the flowering drifts rather than sit in a separate block of its own.
    • 26 × Little Bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, 2–4 feet) — 18 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  8. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 28 × Scarlet Globemallow (Sphaeralcea coccinea, 6–12 inches) — 15 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Finally, scatter the self-sowing fillers into the gaps. Tuck them wherever there is still a hole. They are short-lived on purpose: they cover bare ground for the first two seasons while the permanent plants knit together, then fade out as the bed closes.
    • 3 × Deerweed (Acmispon glaber, 2–4 feet) — 30 inches apart (about 2.5 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  10. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  11. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

Do not spray anything, ever, including organic Bt or spinosad. Leave milkweed stalks standing over winter.

Your calendar — zone 8
  • Main cut-back window: early to mid March. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: late March. Typical first autumn frost: mid November.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 8. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Agaves, yuccas and other rosettes — never cut back
Red Yucca

There is no cutting back, ever. Cutting the leaves destroys the shape permanently, because each rosette grows from a single central point. Pull off only the dry, papery lower leaves, and saw the spent flower stalk off near the base once it has dried. Keep mulch and groundcover pulled back from the crown so water drains away from it.

Watering: Almost none, and overwatering is the real danger. Water once a month in the first summer only, then leave them to the rain. Never let water stand in the centre of a rosette, and never run an irrigation line to one.

Warm-season grasses — one hard cut a year
Little Bluestem

These are the plants the phrase “cut the bed back” really applies to. Leave them standing all winter for structure and seed, then in early to mid March, before the new shoots are more than an inch or two high, cut the whole clump to 4–6 inches. Hedge shears or a string trimmer are fine. Cutting after growth starts leaves the clump with brown tips all season.

Watering: Low. Water weekly through the first summer only. After that these are among the most drought-proof plants in the bed, and watering them does more harm than good: it makes the clumps grow soft and flop open by late summer.

Evergreen perennials — tidy only, do not cut to the ground
Pineneedle Milkweed

These hold living leaves through winter and will be slow to recover if sheared hard. In early to mid March, pull or snip out only the dead and blackened leaves. Cut the spent flower stems off at the base. Every third year you can shear the top third to force fresh growth from the crown.

Watering: Average, but do not let them go bone dry in winter. Evergreen leaves keep losing water in cold weather, so in a long dry winter spell give them one soak while the ground is unfrozen.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
Havard's Penstemon, California Goldenrod, Parry's Penstemon, Engelmann Daisy, Gregg's Mistflower, Golden Prairie Clover

Leave every stem standing all winter. In early to mid March, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Scarlet Globemallow

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In early to mid March, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

Self-sowing fillers — decide where the seedlings go
Deerweed

These are short-lived by design and carry the bed while the slower plants fill in. Let the seedheads stand through winter for the birds. In early to mid March, shake the stems over any gap you want colonised, then cut them down. Through the season, pull seedlings out of the places you do not want them while they are still small.

Watering: Low. Water enough in the first few weeks to get them going, then leave them alone. Plants kept slightly lean set more seed, which for this layer is the whole point.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Plant once and never move: Engelmann Daisy, Golden Prairie Clover. These make a deep taproot and rarely survive being dug up and relocated. Buy them small.
  • Must have sharp drainage — these rot in damp soil: Havard's Penstemon. If your bed holds water after rain, plant these on a slight mound or mix a few inches of grit into their planting holes. Keep mulch off their crowns entirely, and water them less often than the rest of the bed.
  • Spreads and will need editing: California Goldenrod, Gregg's Mistflower. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 156 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 250 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for a dry bed
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: one deep soak a week in hot weather, and skip it whenever the soil is damp two inches down. Err on the dry side from the start.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every three or four weeks during a heat wave, and otherwise nothing.
  • Year 3 onward: stop watering entirely. Continued summer irrigation is the main way established dry-soil plantings are lost.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once a week for the first summer only, then stop. These species fail from too much water far more often than too little. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in early to mid March, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Monarch Watch certifies waystations of 100 sq ft or larger carrying at least ten milkweed plants of two or more species plus continuous nectar.

Plant-by-plant notes
  • Penstemon havardii (Havard's Penstemon) — Tall red spires over glaucous paddle leaves, from the Chihuahuan Desert. Needs sharp drainage. Looks like: 3–6 feet tall, a tall flowering spire, with red flowers from April to June. Hardy in zones 7–9; family Plantaginaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Hesperaloe parviflora (Red Yucca) — An evergreen strappy fountain with 5-foot coral spikes. A hummingbird magnet all summer. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, a stiff, spiky architectural rosette, with coral flowers from April to September. Hardy in zones 5–11; family Asparagaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Solidago velutina subsp. californica (California Goldenrod) — Plumes of gold in late summer when little else blooms in California. Spreads modestly. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, an arching, fountain-like clump, with yellow flowers from July to October. Hardy in zones 7–10; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Penstemon parryi (Parry's Penstemon) — Rose-pink spires in late winter, timed for the desert hummingbirds. Short lived but reseeds. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, a tall flowering spire, with pink flowers from February to April. Hardy in zones 8–10; family Plantaginaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Asclepias linaria (Pineneedle Milkweed) — A shrubby milkweed with needle-like evergreen leaves, flowering much of the year. Looks like: 1–3 feet tall, a finely textured, almost ferny plant, with white flowers from March to October. Hardy in zones 8–10; family Apocynaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Engelmannia peristenia (Engelmann Daisy) — Deeply cut leaves and yellow daisies held well above them. Deep taproot. Looks like: 1.5–3 feet tall, a bushy clump topped with daisy flowers, with yellow flowers from March to July. Hardy in zones 5–9; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Conoclinium greggii (Gregg's Mistflower) — The famous Queen butterfly magnet, with lacy leaves and fuzzy lavender heads. Spreads by rhizome. Looks like: 1–2 feet tall, a rounded, bushy mound, with lavender flowers from April to November. Hardy in zones 7–10; family Asteraceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Dalea aurea (Golden Prairie Clover) — Silky thimbles of golden flowers on grey stems. Taproot. Looks like: 1–2 feet tall, slender stems with thimble-shaped flower heads, with yellow flowers from June to August. Hardy in zones 5–9; family Fabaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Schizachyrium scoparium (Little Bluestem) — Blue-green in summer, copper-orange in winter with silver seed. The best matrix grass. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, a stiff, erect clump, with bronze seedheads in August and September. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Poaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Sphaeralcea coccinea (Scarlet Globemallow) — Orange cups over silvery leaves on a low spreading plant. Needs lean dry soil. Looks like: 6–12 inches tall, a low, wide-spreading plant, with orange flowers from May to August. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Malvaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Acmispon glaber (Deerweed) — A short-lived pioneer of burned chaparral that hosts many blues and hairstreaks. Looks like: 2–4 feet tall, an airy, see-through plant on fine stems, with yellow flowers from March to August. Hardy in zones 8–10; family Fabaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild

How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Choose one sedge as a unifying carpet and plant it 10 inches apart across the whole bed, then set ferns in loose groups of three to seven and drop clumps of shade perennials into the gaps. Texture does the work that flower colour does in sun.

When to plant — zone 8, Pacific Northwest (west of the Cascades)
Best windowAutumn, as soon as the first steady rains arrive — roughly October to late November.
Second choiceLate winter is a workable second choice. Avoid spring and summer entirely.
Why it mattersThis is the single most important decision you will make with these plants. The native flora here grows through the wet winter and sleeps through the dry summer, so autumn planting lets the winter rains do the establishment watering for you. Plant in spring and you commit yourself to irrigating all summer, which is what kills drought-adapted natives more often than drought ever does.
Your frost datesLast spring frost is typically late March and first autumn frost mid November in zone 8. These are regional averages — look up your own at frost dates by ZIP code, and treat your state Cooperative Extension planting calendar as the final word.
BuyingOrder plugs or quart pots in late winter for autumn delivery, since good native nurseries sell out of the better species months ahead. Small plants establish faster than large ones and cost a fraction as much — resist buying the biggest pot available.
Step by step
  1. Clear the ground and leave the soil alone. Kill or strip the existing turf and weeds completely — smother it under cardboard for a season, or lift the sod. Loosen only the top 2–3 inches so you can get a trowel in. Do not add fertiliser, and do not dig in compost deeper than a couple of inches. These are species adapted to ordinary unimproved soil; rich beds make them grow soft and flop. This bed is 12 feet by 5 feet, which is 60 square feet and takes 76 plants of 5 species, about 1.3 plants per square foot.
  2. Look each plant up before you buy it. Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 3 × False Solomon's Seal (Maianthemum racemosum, 2–3 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  6. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 5 × Large-leaf Avens (Geum macrophyllum, 1–3 feet) — 12 inches apart, as one drift of about 5 plants.
    • 5 × Western Trillium (Trillium ovatum, 8–18 inches) — 12 inches apart, as one drift of about 5 plants.
  7. Place the ferns in loose groups of three to seven. Tuck them where they will be shaded in the afternoon, and against the base of taller plants rather than out in the open.
    • 13 × Western Maidenhair Fern (Adiantum aleuticum, 1–2 feet) — 15 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  8. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 50 × Woodland Strawberry (Fragaria vesca, 4–8 inches) — 10 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  10. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

No mulch and no leaf removal. Cut deciduous ferns down in late winter; shear evergreen sedges to 3 inches in early spring every second or third year.

Your calendar — zone 8
  • Main cut-back window: early to mid March. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: late March. Typical first autumn frost: mid November.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 8. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Deciduous ferns — remove old fronds before the new ones uncurl
Western Maidenhair Fern

The fronds collapse over winter and protect the crown, so leave them. Cut them off at the base in early to mid March, before the new fiddleheads unroll. Once the fiddleheads are up, cutting anywhere near them damages the whole season's growth.

Watering: The highest need in the bed. Ferns have little ability to hold water and crisp irreversibly once they dry out. Keep the soil evenly damp but never waterlogged, and water in any dry spell longer than about ten days, even years later.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
False Solomon's Seal, Large-leaf Avens

Leave every stem standing all winter. In early to mid March, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Woodland Strawberry

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In early to mid March, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

Plants that go dormant — leave them alone and mark where they are
Western Trillium

These disappear completely for part of the year. That is normal and does not mean they have died. Push a labelled stake in beside each one before it fades, so you do not weed, dig or plant into the crown while it is invisible. Never water a summer-dormant plant to try to revive it.

Watering: Only while they are visibly in growth. Once the leaves yellow and the plant goes dormant, stop completely, because watering a dormant crown rots it. This is why everything planted around them has to tolerate the same dry rest.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Spreads and will need editing: Woodland Strawberry. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 37 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 60 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for average soil
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: roughly that inch a week, counting rainfall, tapering off as autumn cools.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every two or three weeks during drought only. The bed should be largely self-sufficient by now.
  • Year 3 onward: water only in an exceptional drought, and even then only the ferns and the moisture-lovers. Everything else should be on its own.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
These will want water first and show it soonest: Large-leaf Avens, Western Maidenhair Fern. Use them as your indicator plants — when they wilt in the evening rather than perking back up, the bed needs a soak.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once or twice a week through the first growing season, then taper off. A long soak twice a week beats a daily sprinkle: it drives roots downward. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in early to mid March, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Carex is among the most important larval host genera for skippers and satyrs, and a dense sedge carpet outcompetes garlic mustard and stiltgrass.

Plant-by-plant notes
  • Maianthemum racemosum (False Solomon's Seal) — Plumes of white become ruby berries. A strong arching form for the shade middle ground. Looks like: 2–3 feet tall, an arching, fountain-like clump, with white flowers in May and June. Hardy in zones 3–9; family Asparagaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Geum macrophyllum (Large-leaf Avens) — Small yellow flowers and burred seedheads for moist shade. Looks like: 1–3 feet tall, a stiff, erect clump, with yellow flowers from May to July. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Rosaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Trillium ovatum (Western Trillium) — The western white trillium, ageing to pink. Buy nursery-propagated stock; dormant by late summer. Looks like: 8–18 inches tall, a stiff, erect clump, with white flowers from March to May. Hardy in zones 5–8; family Melanthiaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild
  • Adiantum aleuticum (Western Maidenhair Fern) — Black stems and fans of pale green leaflets for moist shade and seeps. Looks like: 1–2 feet tall, a finely textured, almost ferny plant, grown for its foliage. Hardy in zones 3–8; family Pteridaceae. photos & full profile · photos in the wild

How to lay this bed out, plant it and look after it — step by step
Design intent

Build the composition from leaf shape, not flower colour: set one bold, broad-leaved or arching species against a fine-textured fern and a strappy sedge, then repeat that trio three or four times down the bed. Keep flowers pale so they read in low light.

When to plant — zone 8, Pacific Northwest (west of the Cascades)
Best windowAutumn, as soon as the first steady rains arrive — roughly October to late November.
Second choiceLate winter is a workable second choice. Avoid spring and summer entirely.
Why it mattersThis is the single most important decision you will make with these plants. The native flora here grows through the wet winter and sleeps through the dry summer, so autumn planting lets the winter rains do the establishment watering for you. Plant in spring and you commit yourself to irrigating all summer, which is what kills drought-adapted natives more often than drought ever does.
Your frost datesLast spring frost is typically late March and first autumn frost mid November in zone 8. These are regional averages — look up your own at frost dates by ZIP code, and treat your state Cooperative Extension planting calendar as the final word.
BuyingOrder plugs or quart pots in late winter for autumn delivery, since good native nurseries sell out of the better species months ahead. Small plants establish faster than large ones and cost a fraction as much — resist buying the biggest pot available.
Step by step
  1. Clear the ground and leave the soil alone. Kill or strip the existing turf and weeds completely — smother it under cardboard for a season, or lift the sod. Loosen only the top 2–3 inches so you can get a trowel in. Do not add fertiliser, and do not dig in compost deeper than a couple of inches. These are species adapted to ordinary unimproved soil; rich beds make them grow soft and flop. This bed is 12 feet by 5 feet, which is 60 square feet and takes 58 plants of 5 species, about one plant for every 1.0 square feet.
  2. Look each plant up before you buy it. Every species in the table above carries two photo links — one to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center for curated photographs and a full profile, one to iNaturalist for photographs of the plant growing wild, which shows you honestly how it will look rather than how a catalogue stages it. Check the habit and the mature size against the space you have, because the commonest regret with a native bed is a plant that turns out twice the size the label implied.
  3. Mark the front edge. Everything below depends on knowing which side you look at the bed from. Lay a hose or string along that edge; the plan above is drawn with the front edge along the bottom. If the bed is an island you can walk all the way around, treat the long centre line as the “back” and mirror the tall plants out toward both faces.
  4. Mark out the drifts before you plant anything. Copy the shapes from the plan onto the ground freehand with a line of flour, sand or marking paint. Do not measure them: they are meant to be irregular. Stand back and look from the front edge, and from a window if the bed is seen from indoors, before you commit. Every spacing given below is centre to centre — measured from the middle of one plant to the middle of the next, not from leaf to leaf, and not the width of the gap between them.
  5. Set out the tall structure first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 3 × False Solomon's Seal (Maianthemum racemosum, 2–3 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), as 3 individual plants, set well apart rather than in a clump.
  6. Set out the shrub backbone first, along the back third. These are the biggest plants and everything else is arranged around them, so position them before anything goes in the ground. Space them so that at maturity their canopies just touch. Stand each pot in place, look from the front, and adjust before you dig.
    • 1 × Salal (Gaultheria shallon, 2–5 feet) — 36 inches apart (about 3 feet), as a single specimen.
  7. Now place the flowering drifts, working from tallest to shortest. Each species goes in as a long tapering drift rather than a round blob or a single dot, and the drift should run along the length of the bed. Keep the shorter species toward the front so nothing is hidden. Repeat at least one species in two or three separate places — that repetition is what makes a planting read as deliberate.
    • 11 × Large-leaf Avens (Geum macrophyllum, 1–3 feet) — 12 inches apart, in 2 separate drifts of about 6 plants each.
  8. Place the ferns in loose groups of three to seven. Tuck them where they will be shaded in the afternoon, and against the base of taller plants rather than out in the open.
    • 3 × Lady Fern (Athyrium filix-femina, 2–3 feet) — 24 inches apart (about 2 feet), planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  9. Carpet the remaining ground with the groundcover carpet — this is the step that gets skipped, and the one that decides whether the bed succeeds. Plant it across the whole bed, right up to the crowns of everything already planted and all the way to the front edge, so that no bare soil is left anywhere. On the plan this is the layer filling every gap between the taller drifts. A closed green carpet is what suppresses weeds and means you never have to buy mulch again.
    • 40 × Woodland Strawberry (Fragaria vesca, 4–8 inches) — 10 inches apart, planted continuously across the ground rather than in clumps.
  10. Plant, then water in hard. Set every plant at exactly the depth it was in its pot — burying the crown is the most common cause of losses. Firm the soil around each one and water immediately and generously, enough to settle the soil right down through the root ball. Autumn planting establishes better than spring almost everywhere, because the roots grow while the top is dormant.
  11. Mulch thinly, once, and only this year. Put down no more than 1–2 inches of leaf mould or fine bark, only in the gaps between the plants, and keep it off the crowns. This is a one-off to get you through the first year; from the second year the groundcover layer is your mulch. After that, resist the annual urge to re-mulch: a fresh layer every spring smothers the self-sowers and the groundcover, and it is the reason many native beds never fill in.
Maintenance philosophy

No mulch once the groundcover knits. Cut deciduous material down in late winter and top-dress with leaf mould, never bark.

Your calendar — zone 8
  • Main cut-back window: early to mid March. Wait as late as you can bear. The signal is several consecutive days near 50°F, when insects are leaving the old stems and the first new shoots show at the base.
  • Typical last spring frost here: late March. Typical first autumn frost: mid November.
  • Cut nothing in autumn. The dead stems and seedheads are the winter habitat and the bird food, and they are most of what this planting is for.
  • These are regional averages for zone 8. Look up your own dates: frost dates by ZIP code · NOAA climate normals · or search for your state's Cooperative Extension planting calendar, which is the most locally accurate of the three.
What to do with each kind of plant in this bed
Spring-flowering shrubs — prune right after they bloom, or not at all
Salal

Never cut these back with the perennials: the flower buds for next spring form on this year's wood over summer, so a late-winter cut removes the entire display. Most need no pruning at all. When one outgrows its space, prune within a few weeks of the flowers fading: remove whole stems at the base rather than shearing the outline.

Watering: Deep and infrequent, for two full years. Give each shrub a long slow soak at the root ball once a week through its first two summers rather than a light sprinkle, so the water reaches the bottom of the roots. After that, only in real drought.

Deciduous ferns — remove old fronds before the new ones uncurl
Lady Fern

The fronds collapse over winter and protect the crown, so leave them. Cut them off at the base in early to mid March, before the new fiddleheads unroll. Once the fiddleheads are up, cutting anywhere near them damages the whole season's growth.

Watering: The highest need in the bed. Ferns have little ability to hold water and crisp irreversibly once they dry out. Keep the soil evenly damp but never waterlogged, and water in any dry spell longer than about ten days, even years later.

Herbaceous perennials — cut back in spring, never in autumn
False Solomon's Seal, Large-leaf Avens

Leave every stem standing all winter. In early to mid March, cut the dead stems down to 8–12 inches and leave those stubs in place: native bees nest inside hollow stems, and the new growth hides them within a month. Rake the cut material into a loose pile in a corner for a few weeks so anything still inside can get out, then compost it.

Watering: Average. Through the first season give the equivalent of about an inch of water a week when it has not rained. Once established most need nothing in an ordinary summer, and a deep soak every two or three weeks carries them through a drought.

Low perennials and mats — a light shear, not a cut-back
Woodland Strawberry

These are too short to have stems worth leaving, so the stem-nesting advice does not apply. In early to mid March, run hand shears over them to take off the dead top growth, down to roughly 2–3 inches, and pull out any flattened brown leaves by hand. Never cut into the woody centre of a mat-former, and never bury the crown in mulch.

Watering: Low to average, but check these first in hot weather. Small root systems near the surface dry out before anything else in the bed. Water the soil rather than the foliage, and keep mulch off the crowns so they do not rot.

Jobs that apply only to particular species here
  • Spreads and will need editing: Woodland Strawberry. Walk the edges once each spring and pull back anything that has moved further than you want. This is five minutes of work if done annually, and a rescue job if left for three years.
How much to water
The rule of thumb, in real numbers
  • “An inch of water” for this bed is about 37 gallons. One inch over one square foot is 0.62 gallons, and your bed is 60 square feet. That is the figure to aim at in a week with no rain during the first season.
  • Measure it, do not guess. Stand a straight-sided tin — a tuna or cat-food can is ideal — in the bed while you water, and stop when it has an inch in it. That tells you how long your hose or sprinkler needs, and you only have to do it once. A $5 rain gauge then tells you how much of the week's inch the weather already supplied.
  • Check before watering. Push a finger two inches into the soil. Damp means wait. This single habit prevents most of the losses in a new bed, because overwatering kills more native plants than drought does — constantly damp soil suffocates and rots the roots.
  • Water deeply and rarely, never lightly and often. One long soak drives roots down; daily sprinkling keeps them in the top inch, where they die the first time you go away for a fortnight. Water early in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves.
Schedule for average soil
  • Weeks 1 to 2: water every second or third day, whatever the season. Nothing has roots outside its own root ball yet.
  • Weeks 3 to 8: twice a week if it has not rained.
  • Rest of year 1: roughly that inch a week, counting rainfall, tapering off as autumn cools.
  • Year 2: a deep soak every two or three weeks during drought only. The bed should be largely self-sufficient by now.
  • Year 3 onward: water only in an exceptional drought, and even then only the ferns and the moisture-lovers. Everything else should be on its own.
  • New plants added later start this schedule again from week one, even if the rest of the bed needs nothing.
These will want water first and show it soonest: Large-leaf Avens, Lady Fern. Use them as your indicator plants — when they wilt in the evening rather than perking back up, the bed needs a soak.
If you install irrigation, use drip line or soaker hose under the planting rather than overhead spray. Overhead watering wets foliage, encourages mildew on beebalm and phlox, and wastes most of the water to evaporation. Put it on a manual valve, not a timer: a timer waters during rain, which is how beds drown.
The first three years
  • Year 1 — water and weed. Water deeply once or twice a week through the first growing season, then taper off. A long soak twice a week beats a daily sprinkle: it drives roots downward. Weed every two or three weeks; the bed is open now and weeds will out-run your plants if you let them seed.
  • Year 1 — expect it to look sparse. It is supposed to. The plants are spaced to close up, not to look finished on day one. Do not fill the gaps with extra plants, and do not widen the spacing to make it look full sooner.
  • Year 2 — the groundcover closes. Weeding drops sharply once the carpet knits. Keep going round the edges, which is where new weeds arrive.
  • Year 3 and on — edit rather than maintain. Move or remove what has overstepped, shift seedlings you like into gaps, replace anything that died. Divide clump-forming grasses every four or five years, in early to mid March, once the centre of the clump goes hollow.
  • Never fertilise. It produces soft, floppy growth, shortens the life of most of these species, and feeds weeds more than plants.
  • Never use insecticide, including organic ones. Bt and spinosad kill caterpillars, which are the point of the bed. Chewed leaves are the planting working, not failing.
Why it works ecologically

Deep shade beds are where most caterpillars pupate. A closed herbaceous layer plus retained leaf litter completes a life cycle that a bare mulched bed interrupts.
